meaning: “Without even doing …”: someone skips even the most basic step and goes straight to something else. Usually carries criticism, annoyance, or surprise.
connection: Verb masu-stem / suru-noun + もしないで (written: もせずに)

senses.label: Without even … (criticism)
senses.meaning: The most basic thing that should be done is skipped, and the next action happens anyway. The speaker usually sounds critical. 「も」 adds the sense of “not even this much”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + もしないで (見もしないで, 聞きもしないで); suru-noun + もしないで (確認もしないで)
examples: He started using the machine without even reading the manual.
Throwing it away without even looking inside — that's awful.
I ended up submitting the documents without even checking them.

senses.label: Not even stopping to … (devotion)
senses.meaning: Someone is so absorbed in something that they skip basics like sleeping or eating. This stresses their effort or dedication, so it is not always criticism.
senses.connection: 寝もしないで / 休みもしないで / 食べもしないで + verb
examples: My mother looked after me when I had a fever, without even sleeping.
He kept working all day without even taking a break.

senses.label: Written form: もせずに
senses.meaning: The written version of 「もしないで」 is 「もせずに」 or 「もせず」. Same meaning; common in news and novels.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem / suru-noun + もせず(に)
examples: He walked away without even looking back.
Drawing conclusions without proper research is dangerous.

notes: Put 「も」 between the verb masu-stem (without ます) and 「しない」: ✕「見るもしないで」✕「見ないもで」→ ○「見もしないで」. With suru-verbs, put 「も」 after the noun: ○「確認もしないで」.

When you simply report “did B without doing A” in a neutral way, do not add 「も」. To say neutrally “left without eating breakfast”, use 「朝ご飯を食べないで出かけた」; saying 「食べもしないで」 adds clear criticism or annoyance.

Using this form to describe someone's behavior amounts to accusing them to their face of not doing even the bare minimum. Saying 「資料を読みもしないで……」 to a superior or a client is very rude. When you need to raise the issue, use a softer phrasing such as 「ご確認いただけましたでしょうか」.

「何もしないで」 (doing nothing) is a full negation with a question word + も, and 「一時間もしないうちに」 (in less than an hour) is quantity + も. They look the same but are not this grammar point, and their meanings are completely different.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A mother complains that her child hands in homework without checking it.
daily.example: This kid hands in homework without even looking it over.

daily.title: Teasing a friend
daily.description: Your friend says it's impossible without trying, and you push back.
daily.example: Don't say it's impossible when you haven't even tried.

daily.title: Thanking for care
daily.description: Telling a friend how your family looked after you in hospital.
daily.example: While I was in hospital, my dad came every day without even taking a rest.

work.title: A boss scolds a subordinate
work.description: A subordinate sent an email without checking it.
work.example: Please stop sending emails without even checking the content.

work.title: Reading a news report
work.description: A report criticizes a company's hasty decision.
work.example: The company reportedly pushed ahead with the plan without sufficient review.

etymology: The masu-stem (used like a noun) + the emphatic particle 「も」 + 「しない」 + 「で」 (“in a state of not doing”). 「も」 singles out the action — “not even this” — giving “without even doing …”.

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: 「〜ないで」 simply says “do B without doing A” and passes no judgment. 「〜もしないで」 adds 「も」 to stress “didn't even do something as basic as A”, and often carries reproach or surprise.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: 「〜ずに」 is the written form of 「〜ないで」 and is equally neutral. 「もせずに」 is the written form of 「もしないで」 and keeps its “not even” emphasis and tone of reproach.

similar.title: 〜もしない (not even)
similar.explanation: Both come from the same source, masu-stem + 「も」 + 「しない」. 「〜もしない」 ends the sentence and only says “doesn't even do …”; 「〜もしないで」 must be followed by another action, meaning “without even doing …, (did B)”.

similar.title: 〜ことなく
similar.explanation: 「〜ことなく」 also means “without doing …”, but it is a written, neutral statement, often used with positive evaluation, as in 「休むことなく働いた」. 「〜もしないで」 is more colloquial and mostly carries reproach.

formation: Formed from “verb masu-stem + 「も」 + 「しない」 + 「で」”. The masu-stem (renyōkei) can itself work as a noun, the emphatic particle 「も」 singles out that action to mean “even this”, and 「しない」 negates it, giving “doesn't even do A”. The final 「で」 turns this into a state modifying the next clause: “in a state of not having even done A, went on to do B”. “Not even doing the bare minimum A” already implies the expectation that A should have been done, so the whole sentence naturally carries reproach or dissatisfaction; when A is a basic need such as sleeping or eating, it instead stresses deep devotion. The written 「もせずに」 simply replaces 「しないで」 with the classical negative 「せず」 + 「に」, and the structure is exactly the same.

meaning: Attaches to a noun to mean “on par with …, at the level of …”, as in 「プロ並み」 or 「平年並み」.
connection: Noun + 並み (の + noun / に / だ)

senses.label: On par with …
senses.meaning: The degree or level is about the same as some standard: “as good as …”, “like a …”. Often used as praise for a level higher than expected.
senses.connection: Noun + 並みの + noun / 並みに + verb or adjective / 並みだ (プロ並み, 大人並み, 一流並み)
examples: His cooking is as good as a professional's.
This child eats as much as an adult.
This hotel offers service on par with a luxury hotel.

senses.label: About the same as usual
senses.meaning: 「平年並み」, 「例年並み」 and 「前年並み」 are set phrases in weather forecasts and statistics. They mean “about the same as an average year / last year”.
senses.connection: 平年 / 例年 / 前年 + 並み
examples: This summer's temperatures are expected to be around normal.
Sales stayed at about the same level as last year.

senses.label: Like ordinary people
senses.meaning: 「人並み」 and 「世間並み」 mean “like most people, ordinary”. Often used modestly about one's own life or ability.
senses.connection: 人並み / 世間並み + の + noun / に
examples: If I can live a normal life, that's enough for me.
I'd like to get married and have a family, like most people.

notes: 「並み」 attaches only to nouns: ✕「上手並み」✕「大人のような並み」→ ○「プロ並み」「大人並み」.

When the benchmark is the “average person”, 「並み」, 「人並み」 and 「並の〜」 themselves mean “ordinary, nothing special”. Telling someone to their face 「腕は並みだね」 or 「並の出来だ」 is belittling and rude. To praise, use a comparison with a high standard such as 「プロ並み」.
「月並み」 means “mediocre, clichéd” (「月並みな表現」 is a criticism), and the 「並み」 in 「町並み」 and 「足並み」 means “a row, arrangement”. Neither means “on a par with …”, so do not guess from the kanji.
「平年並み」 and 「例年並み」 mean “the same as in a normal year” and are neutral statistical expressions, not a verdict of “so-so, neither good nor bad”.

daily.title: Praising a friend's baking
daily.description: A friend serves you a cake they made.
daily.example: This cake is as good as one from a shop.

daily.title: Watching the forecast
daily.description: The weather forecast gives tomorrow's temperature.
daily.example: Tomorrow's high will be around normal for this time of year.

daily.title: Talking about life goals
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about the future.
daily.example: I don't need luxury — just to live like everyone else.

work.title: Evaluating a new hire
work.description: A manager praises a new employee.
work.example: His English is on par with a native speaker's.

work.title: Reading business news
work.description: A report on a company's results.
work.example: Profits this term held at about the same level as last year.

etymology: From the verbs 「並ぶ」 / 「並む」 (to line up). “Standing in the same row” came to mean “on the same level”, and it became a suffix meaning “equal to …”.

similar.title: 〜と並んで
similar.explanation: Both come from 「並ぶ」. 「〜と並んで」 means “alongside …, on a par with …”: the two are equals, and it is mostly used for rankings and standing. 「〜並み」 means “reaching the level of …”, measuring something against the preceding noun.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (degree)
similar.explanation: 「くらい」 can follow verbs, adjectives and more, and expresses degree by comparison, as in 「泣きたいくらい」. 「並み」 attaches only to nouns and means “reaching a certain standard”; 「プロ並み」 cannot be replaced with 「プロくらい」 to give the same complimentary feel.

similar.title: 〜と同じ
similar.explanation: 「と同じ」 means exactly the same, with no evaluative tone. 「並み」 means roughly the same level, and when compared with a high standard it adds a complimentary “on a par with” tone.

formation: 「並み」 is the nominalized renyōkei of the verb 「並む・並ぶ」 (to line up), originally meaning “lined up together”. Attached to a noun as a suffix, 「プロ並み」 literally means “lined up in the same row as professionals”. Being able to stand in the same row means the level is comparable, which yields “on a par with …”. When the benchmark is an average standard such as “ordinary people” or “a normal year” (人並み, 平年並み), the meaning becomes “ordinary, as usual”, and the bare 「並」 even became a grade name meaning “regular, medium”. Since the benchmark is a noun, 「並み」 can attach only to nouns.

meaning: Expresses strong admiration or surprise: “What a …!”, “How …!”, “Believe it or not, …”.
connection: なんという + noun (だ); なんと + adjective / verb + ことか / のだろう

senses.label: What a …!
senses.meaning: 「なんという + noun」 shows strong feeling about something in front of you, good or bad. 「なんということだ」 often means shock or dismay: “How could this happen?”
senses.connection: なんという + noun + だ / でしょう (なんという美しさだ, なんということだ)
examples: What a beautiful view!
Oh no, how could this happen? It's all gone.

senses.label: How …!
senses.meaning: 「なんと〜ことか / のだろう」 pours out emotion. It is written and a bit literary. In speech, 「なんて」 is more common.
senses.connection: なんと + i-adjective / na-adjective / verb + ことか / のだろう / ことだろう
examples: What a wonderful performance!
How precious peaceful everyday life is!

senses.label: Believe it or not
senses.meaning: 「なんと」 at the start of a sentence or before a number shows surprise at something unexpected. Common when reporting a surprising fact.
senses.connection: なんと、+ sentence; なんと + number
examples: Believe it or not, those two are apparently getting married.
A whopping 100,000 people came to this event.

notes: Adding the question 「か」 or a question mark at the end turns it into a real question: 「なんという花ですか」 means “What is this flower called?”. For an exclamation, say 「なんという美しい花だろう」 or 「なんと美しい花だ」.
「なんということだ」 and 「なんということをしてくれたんだ」 express shock and severe reproach. Using them about someone's actions, especially a superior's or a client's, is very rude.
The exclamatory 「なんと」 looks similar to 「なんとか」 (somehow, managed to), 「なんとなく」 (for some reason) and 「なんと言っても」 (after all), but the meaning is far apart; what follows 「なんと」 changes everything.
In everyday conversation people usually say 「なんて」, as in 「なんてきれいなんだろう」. 「なんと素晴らしい……」 sounds exaggerated, as if you were reading aloud or giving a speech.

daily.title: Sightseeing
daily.description: Watching the sunrise from a mountaintop.
daily.example: How beautiful!

daily.title: Sharing big news
daily.description: Telling your family something unexpected.
daily.example: Guess what — I won the lottery!

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character's monologue after a disaster.
daily.example: How could this happen? There's no undoing it now.

work.title: Product promotion
work.description: Ad copy highlights an amazing number.
work.example: In just one month after launch, we sold an incredible one million units.

work.title: Giving a speech
work.description: Expressing thanks at an awards ceremony.
work.example: How reassuring your support has been to me!

etymology: 「なんと」 comes from the question word 「何（なに）」, shortened to 「なん」, plus the particle 「と」; originally “how, in what way”. From the rhetorical “How could this be?” it came to express wonder and surprise. 「なんという」 is literally 「何という」 — “what can one say”.

similar.title: 〜なんて
similar.explanation: Both are related: 「なんて」 is the colloquial form of 「なんと」. 「なんて」 can open a sentence as an exclamation, or follow a clause meaning “to think that … (disdain, surprise)”; 「なんと／なんという」 is more formal and written.

similar.title: 〜ことか
similar.explanation: 「〜ことか」 itself means “how …!”, and it often pairs with 「なんと」 or 「どんなに」: 「なんとありがたいことか」. 「なんと」 at the front introduces the exclamation, and 「ことか」 at the end closes it.

similar.title: 〜とは (surprise)
similar.explanation: 「〜とは」 follows a clause to express shock or surprise at a fact, as in 「彼が犯人だったとは」. 「なんと」 comes first and directly introduces the surprising content, and the two are often used together.

formation: 「なん」 is a sound change of the interrogative 「何（なに）」, and 「と」 is a particle of quotation and manner, so 「なんと」 originally means “how, in what way”. 「なんという」 is 「何と言う」, “what should one say, what should one call it”. When something is so good or so bad that words fail, the speaker voices it as the rhetorical question “how should I put it?”, and that is the source of the exclamation. This is why it often pairs with sentence endings of conjecture or feeling such as 「だろう」 and 「ことか」, turning a “question” into a “sigh”. Standing alone at the start of a sentence, 「なんと」 drops what would follow and keeps only the surprise of “how could this be!”, introducing an unexpected fact.

meaning: “Even after things have gone as far as …, still …”. Usually critical or disapproving.
connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + に至っても

senses.label: Even when it comes to …
senses.meaning: The first part is a serious situation that should prompt action. The second part says nothing changed or no action was taken. Formal and written, often critical or regretful.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に至っても; noun + に至っても (+ なお / まだ)
examples: Even after people died, the company took no safety measures.
Even now that things have come to this, the government won't act.
Even when it went to court, he never apologized.

senses.label: Even now
senses.meaning: 「今に至っても」 and 「今日に至っても」 mean “even now, still …”. It stresses that a state has not changed for a long time.
senses.connection: 今 / 現在 / 今日 + に至っても (+ なお)
examples: The cause of the accident is still unknown even today.
Even now, I can't forget that day.

notes: The second clause must be “still unchanged / still no action”. If it is “only now starting to act”, use 「に至って（はじめて）」: ✕「死者が出るに至っても、ようやく対策が取られた」→ ○「死者が出るに至って、ようやく対策が取られた」. Mixing them up changes the meaning from “still not …” to “only then …”.
Verbs take the dictionary form, not the ta-form: ✕「死者が出たに至っても」→ ○「死者が出るに至っても」.
「に至っては」 (“as for …, it's even worse”, picking an extreme example) differs from 「に至っても」 by a single character and means something entirely different. Do not mix them up.
This is a critical, written-style expression, mostly used when commenting on governments or companies. Saying 「ここに至ってもまだ謝らないのか」 to someone directly is a very harsh reproach.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: A report criticizes a company's response.
daily.example: Even as the damage spread, there was no explanation at all.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: A friend keeps ignoring warnings.
daily.example: Even now that his doctor has told him to stop, he won't quit smoking.

work.title: Opinion article
work.description: A commentator criticizes slow management.
work.example: Even after three straight years of losses, management didn't change course.

work.title: Report
work.description: An investigation notes the problem remains.
work.example: Even now, no fundamental solution has been reached.

etymology: 「至る」 means “to reach”. 「に至って」 is “having reached a certain point”; add the concessive 「ても」 and you get “even having reached this point, …”.

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: Both come from 「至る」. 「に至って（はじめて）」 is sequential: “only when it reached …, then …”; 「に至っても」 is concessive: “even though it has reached this point, still not …”.

similar.title: 〜に至っては
similar.explanation: This also comes from 「至る」. 「に至っては」 picks the most extreme of several examples: “as for …, it's even worse”; 「に至っても」 stresses that the situation is serious yet nothing changes.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: 「にもかかわらず」 is a general concessive, “in spite of …”, and the first part need not be a serious situation. 「に至っても」 stresses that things have gone to an extreme point, and the criticism is stronger.

formation: Formed from “「に」 + 「至って」 + 「も」”. 「至る」 means “to arrive, reach (a place or stage)”, 「に」 marks the arrival point, 「至って」 is its te-form, and 「も」 expresses concession. Together: “even having reached the point of …, still …”. The image of “arriving” implies a situation worsening step by step until it reaches a stage that should have prompted a reaction, so the first part is mostly a serious situation. The concessive 「ても」 shows the result runs against that expectation: nothing has changed, and so the sentence naturally carries criticism or regret. If you replace 「も」 with 「は」 or 「はじめて」, the meaning becomes “as for …” or “only after reaching …” respectively.

meaning: “Associated with …, surrounding …”. Mostly used with legends, stories, and anecdotes.

senses.label: Stories and legends about …
senses.meaning: The most typical use: stories, legends, or secrets that surround a person, place, or object. It has a slightly mysterious, intriguing feel.
senses.connection: Noun + にまつわる + 伝説 / 話 / エピソード / 謎
examples: I heard a strange legend about this temple.
My grandmother told me memories connected to this old clock.

senses.label: Related to …
senses.meaning: Today it is also used broadly for “about …”, often in book titles, TV shows and article headings. It sounds more story-like than 「に関する」.
senses.connection: Noun + にまつわる + トラブル / 問題 / 話題 / 雑学
examples: Trouble involving money happens all around us.
Today, let's talk about topics related to Japanese food.
Here's a story about how the name came about.

notes: It is mainly used to modify “story or topic” nouns such as 「話」「伝説」「噂」「エピソード」「思い出」「トラブル」. In business or legal documents, use 「に関する」 for “concerning”: ✕「契約にまつわる書類を提出してください」→ ○「契約に関する書類」.
It is used almost only in the form 「にまつわる＋noun」: ✕「この寺にまつわって話します」→ ○「この寺について話します」.
The verb 「まつわりつく」 means “to cling to, to pester” (「子どもが母親にまつわりつく」). It looks similar but is not this grammar point, and it carries an annoyed, negative nuance.

daily.title: Sightseeing
daily.description: A guide introduces an old castle to tourists.
daily.example: There's a sad story connected to this castle.

daily.title: Watching TV
daily.description: A friend recommends a trivia show.
daily.example: That show on animal trivia was really interesting.

daily.title: Reading a book
daily.description: A book's title and blurb.
daily.example: This book unravels the mysteries surrounding famous paintings.

work.title: Pitching a feature
work.description: An editor proposes a special feature at a meeting.
work.example: For the next issue, I'd like to run a feature on local festivals.

work.title: Legal consultation
work.description: A law firm's website describes its services.
work.example: We offer consultations on matters related to inheritance.

etymology: 「まつわる」 (纏わる) originally means “to wind around, to cling”. From “winding around something” it came to mean “connected to, surrounding something”.

similar.title: 〜に関して・〜に関する
similar.explanation: 「に関する」 is a neutral, objective “concerning” usable in any formal document; 「にまつわる」 has a narrative feel and mostly goes with legends, anecdotes and memories.

similar.title: 〜にかかわる
similar.explanation: 「にかかわる」 mostly means “affect, bear on (something serious such as life or reputation)”, as in 「命にかかわる病気」; 「にまつわる」 only means “(stories, topics) surrounding …” and does not imply a serious impact.

similar.title: 〜をめぐって
similar.explanation: 「をめぐって」 mostly refers to debate, conflict or competition arising around something, followed by words like 「議論」 or 「対立」; 「にまつわる」 only refers to related stories and topics, without any sense of conflict.

formation: 「まつわる（纏わる）」 originally means “to wind around, to cling to the body”, like a vine twining around a tree trunk. In 「Aにまつわる」, 「に」 marks the thing being wound around, so it literally means “winding around A”. Stories, legends and memories “twine” around a place or object like vines and are handed down through generations, giving the sense “(stories) surrounding A, connected with A”. Because what winds around is something incidental attached to the main subject, it mostly modifies topics like anecdotes and legends rather than the substance of A itself, and that is why it does not suit formal documents.

meaning: “Can't bear to …”: out of pity or attachment, one can't bring oneself to do something.
connection: Verb dictionary form + に忍びない

senses.label: Can't bring oneself to
senses.meaning: Out of sympathy, pity or attachment, one can't bear to do something. Often with 「捨てる」, 「断る」 or 「切る」. Formal and written.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に忍びない (捨てるに忍びない, 断るに忍びない)
examples: These clothes are full of memories, so I can't bear to throw them away.
When she begged me like that, I couldn't bring myself to say no.

senses.label: Too painful to watch / hear
senses.meaning: 「見るに忍びない」 and 「聞くに忍びない」 are set phrases. The scene is so tragic or pitiful that you can't bear to look or listen.
senses.connection: 見る / 聞く + に忍びない
examples: The state of the disaster area was too painful to look at.
The bereaved families' stories were almost too painful to listen to.

notes: The kanji 「忍」 can suggest “endure”, which may mislead you: 「忍びない」 means “cannot bear, cannot find it in one's heart”. 「見るに忍びない」 means “I can't bear to look”, not “I can look at it calmly”.

For pitiful scenes such as disaster victims or sick people, only 「見るに忍びない」 works. If you say 「見るに堪えない」 instead, it means “so bad it's unbearable to look at”, which is seriously rude toward the victims.
It follows the dictionary form of a verb: ✕「捨てたに忍びない」✕「捨てに忍びない」→ ○「捨てるに忍びない」.

daily.title: Decluttering
daily.description: You can't throw away your child's old toys.
daily.example: I can't bear to throw away the toys from when my kids were little.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Talking with family about an injured animal on the news.
daily.example: That puppy was so pitiful I could hardly watch.

work.title: Personnel decision
work.description: A manager talks about layoffs.
work.example: It pains me to let go of employees who served us for years, but there's no other choice.

work.title: Formal letter
work.description: Politely declining a request in a formal letter.
work.example: It truly pains us not to meet your expectations, but we must decline this time.

etymology: 「忍ぶ」 means “to endure, to bear”. 「〜に忍びない」 is literally “cannot endure doing …”, so “can't bear to”. 「忍びない」 alone can also mean “to feel bad about”.

similar.title: 〜に堪えない
similar.explanation: 「見るに堪えない」 means something is so bad or ugly it is unbearable to look at, with disgust or criticism; 「見るに忍びない」 means it is so pitiful you cannot bear to look, with sympathy. The objects differ, and misusing them is very rude.

similar.title: 〜がたい
similar.explanation: 「〜がたい」 means “hard to …”, as in 「捨てがたい」 and 「信じがたい」, and can arise from various reasons; 「に忍びない」 refers specifically to being unable to do something out of sympathy or pity, with stronger emotion.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: 「〜かねる」 means “find it difficult to …” because of one's position or conditions, and is often used to refuse politely in business, as in 「お受けしかねます」; 「に忍びない」 means being unable to do something for emotional reasons, so it cannot be used to refuse a client.

formation: Formed from “「に」 + 「忍び」 + 「ない」”. 「忍ぶ」 means “to endure, to bear”, 「忍び」 is its renyōkei, and adding 「ない」 makes the adjective 「忍びない」, “cannot bear”. The 「に」 means “regarding (the act of …)”, and the dictionary form of the verb works as a noun here. Together: “regarding doing …, my heart cannot bear it”, that is, “cannot bring oneself to do …”. It has a flavor of sympathy and pity because what one cannot bear is not physical pain but the heartache the action would cause, so it mostly goes with actions that hurt to perform, such as 「見る」「聞く」「捨てる」「断る」.

meaning: Says that an explanation, plan or approach is “a stretch, unreasonable, doesn't hold up”.
connection: Noun + には無理がある; verb dictionary form / plain form + の(に)は無理がある

senses.label: Far-fetched, doesn't add up
senses.meaning: An explanation, interpretation or premise is not logical. Used to disagree or criticize politely.
senses.connection: Noun + には無理がある (説明, 設定, 解釈, 理屈); 〜と考えるのには無理がある
examples: I think that explanation is a bit of a stretch.
It's hard to believe he did it all by himself.
The premise of this drama is far-fetched.

senses.label: Unrealistic, hard to pull off
senses.meaning: A plan or schedule is hard to achieve under the conditions. Softer than saying 「無理だ」 outright.
senses.connection: Noun + に(は)無理がある (計画, 日程, 予算); verb dictionary form + には無理がある
examples: Planning to finish it in one week is unrealistic.
Covering everything with this budget is a stretch.

notes: It is only a few characters away from 「〜のも無理はない」 yet means the opposite: 「怒るのも無理はない」 = “no wonder he's angry” (agreement), while 「その説明には無理がある」 = “that explanation doesn't hold up” (rejection).
It evaluates the claim, plan or setup itself as unreasonable; it does not say that a person “can't do” something: ✕「この仕事は彼には無理がある」→ ○「この仕事は彼には無理だ」.
It is softer than 「無理だ」, but in a meeting, telling a superior or client 「この計画には無理があります」 outright still sounds blunt. Usually add a cushion: 「少し無理があるかもしれません」 or 「やや厳しいかと存じます」.

daily.title: Discussing a movie with friends
daily.description: Complaining about the plot after a film.
daily.example: The twist that the culprit was a twin is way too far-fetched.

daily.title: Family plans
daily.description: The family discusses weekend plans.
daily.example: Isn't visiting three places in one day a bit much?

work.title: Raising a concern in a meeting
work.description: Politely voicing concern about a boss's schedule.
work.example: I'm afraid this schedule may be somewhat unrealistic.

work.title: Peer review
work.description: A reviewer points out a problem in a paper's reasoning.
work.example: Drawing this conclusion from these data is a stretch.

etymology: 「無理」 literally means “without reason (理)”, i.e. “unreasonable”, and extends to “impossible, forced”. 「〜には無理がある」 is literally “there is something unreasonable in …”.

similar.title: 〜のも無理はない
similar.explanation: Both use 「無理」. 「のも無理はない」 means “no wonder, understandable”, showing understanding and agreement; 「には無理がある」 means “unreasonable, a stretch”, showing rejection.

similar.title: 〜ことにはならない
similar.explanation: 「〜ことにはならない」 means “that doesn't mean …”, denying a certain inference; 「には無理がある」 points out that the claim or plan itself is far-fetched or unreasonable.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: 「わけがない」 strongly denies on logical grounds, “there's no way”; 「には無理がある」 only softly points out that something “doesn't quite hold up, is a bit of a stretch”, and is much milder.

formation: 「無理」 is made of 「無（none）」 + 「理（reason）」, originally “no reason, unreasonable”, extended to “forced, impossible”. In 「Aには無理がある」, 「に」 marks the place of existence, 「は」 makes A the topic, and 「無理がある」 uses an existence pattern to treat “the unreasonable part” as a concrete thing. Literally: “inside A there is something unreasonable”. Because it says there is a problem within A rather than “A is no good”, it is softer than 「Aは無理だ」 and only points out a partial flaw, which suits polite rebuttal and criticism.

meaning: The same noun is repeated to mean “… after …, over and over”, stressing accumulation.
connection: Noun A + に + noun A + を重ねて / を重ねる

senses.label: Repeated effort
senses.meaning: Effort, study or improvement is made again and again. Used to show a result was hard-won. Often followed by 「〜た結果」, 「〜た末に」 or 「完成した」.
senses.connection: 改良 / 検討 / 工夫 / 苦労 / 練習 + に + the same noun + を重ねて
examples: After improvement upon improvement, the new product was finally finished.
After careful deliberation, we decided to cancel the plan.
Through hardship after hardship, he grew his shop.

senses.label: Going from bad to worse
senses.meaning: With negative things, bad things pile up and get worse — like telling more lies to cover a lie.
senses.connection: 嘘 / 失敗 / 借金 / 無理 + に + the same noun + を重ねる
examples: He piled lie upon lie and finally lost everyone's trust.
I want to escape a life of borrowing to pay off borrowing.

notes: The two nouns must be the same: ✕「研究に努力を重ねて」→ ○「研究に研究を重ねて」「努力に努力を重ねて」.
「年を重ねる」「回を重ねる」「経験を重ねる」 simply mean “accumulate”. They have no repeated 「AにA」 shape and no “emphatic repetition” feel, so they are not this grammar point.
With negative nouns such as 「嘘」「借金」「失敗」, it means “sinking deeper and deeper”. Saying 「嘘に嘘を重ねている」 about someone is a very strong accusation, so mind the situation.

daily.title: Talking about a parent's efforts
daily.description: Telling a friend how your father opened his shop.
daily.example: My dad went through hardship after hardship to open this shop.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character keeps lying and gets trapped.
daily.example: As he piled lie upon lie, he reached the point of no return.

work.title: Product launch
work.description: The lead developer describes the development process.
work.example: This is a product we're proud of — the result of our team's trial and error and countless improvements.

work.title: Company announcement
work.description: A company announces a difficult decision.
work.example: After extensive discussions, we have decided to withdraw from this business.

etymology: 「重ねる」 means “to stack, to repeat”. 「AにAを重ねる」 is literally “stack another A on top of A”, a vivid way to show repeated build-up.

similar.title: 〜に〜て／〜に〜た (emphatic repetition)
similar.explanation: The structures are similar: both repeat the same word with 「に」 for emphasis. 「待ちに待った」 and 「考えに考えた」 repeat a verb stem to stress the degree of the action; 「〜に〜を重ねて」 repeats a noun to stress accumulating times.

similar.title: 〜ては (repetition)
similar.explanation: 「〜ては〜」 also expresses repetition, as in 「書いては消し、書いては消す」, focusing on two actions alternating; 「〜に〜を重ねて」 focuses on the same thing piling up again and again.

similar.title: 〜末(に)
similar.explanation: 「末に」 means “after …, finally”, focusing on the result after a long process, and often combines with this grammar point: 「検討に検討を重ねた末に」. 「〜に〜を重ねて」 itself stresses the repeated process.

formation: 「重ねる」 means “to pile things up layer by layer”. In 「AにAを重ねる」, 「に」 marks the place where something is stacked and 「を」 marks the thing stacked, so it literally means “stack another A on A”. Repeating the same noun before and after is like stacking layers, vividly expressing “again and again, continually accumulating”. The more that is stacked, the heavier it becomes: with effort or improvement it means the result was hard-won; with lies or debt it means they keep piling up and you sink deeper.

meaning: A muttering to oneself in which the speaker cannot make sense of or be sure about something, with doubt, worry or resignation: “I wonder … / who knows ….” Used with question words (のやら), for being at a loss what to do (ものやら), and for worry about the future (ことやら).
connection: (Question word …) verb / adjective plain form, na-adjective / noun + な + のやら／ものやら／ことやら

senses.label: I wonder ...
senses.meaning: Used at the end of a sentence as a self-directed question. Usually pairs with question words like 「何」, 「どこ」, 「いつ」, 「どう」. Carries worry, resignation, or mild annoyance.
senses.connection: Question word + plain form + のやら (どこへ行ったのやら, 何を考えているのやら)
examples: Where on earth did that kid go, I wonder.
I have no idea what he's thinking.
Who knows when this construction will ever finish.

senses.label: What should I do? (ものやら)
senses.meaning: 「〜たものやら」 and 「〜ばいいものやら」 mean not knowing what to do; being at a loss.
senses.connection: どう + verb ta-form + ものやら; どう + verb ば-form + いいものやら
examples: How on earth should I explain this situation?
I have no idea where to even begin.

senses.label: What will become of it? (ことやら)
senses.meaning: 「どうなることやら」 and 「いつになることやら」 are set phrases. They express worry or pessimism about the future.
senses.connection: どうなる / いつになる + ことやら; いつのことやら
examples: I'm so worried about what will happen from here.
Who knows when the house will ever be finished.

senses.label: Inserted clause
senses.meaning: 「〜のやら」 plus a comma works as an aside: "Who knows how, but ..." The following clause states what actually happened.
senses.connection: Question word + plain form + のやら、+ main clause
examples: Who knows where she heard it, but my mother already knew about my marriage.
Who knows who started it, but that rumor is spreading.

senses.label: ... or ...?
senses.meaning: 「〜のやら〜のやら」 sets two possibilities side by side: "Is it A or B? I can't tell." Often used when someone's attitude is ambiguous.
senses.connection: Plain form + のやら + plain form + のやら
examples: I can't tell from his face whether he's happy or angry.

notes: 「〜のやら」is a doubt you voice to yourself, so you can't use it to ask the listener a question: ✕「明日は何時に来るのやら？」(asking the other person) → ○「明日は何時に来ますか」.

It carries resignation or annoyance. Saying 「部長は何を考えているのやら」 is effectively a dig at the person, and would be very rude if your boss or a client overheard it. Keep it for private talk among people you know well.
Don't confuse it with the adverbs 「何やら」("something or other") and 「どうやら」("apparently"): 「何やら音がする」means "I hear some kind of sound," not "I wonder."
To express doubt, 「やら」must follow 「の」(or 「もの」/「こと」). 「本やらノートやら」is only a list of examples and has no "I wonder" meaning.
「ものやら」 is mostly used in 「〜たものやら」 and 「〜ばいいものやら」 (“I don't know what to do”), and 「ことやら」 in 「どうなることやら」 and 「いつになることやら」 (worry about the future). Do not swap these set patterns freely.

daily.title: Worried about a child
daily.description: A mother worries because her child is home late.
daily.example: Where is he and what is he doing at this hour?

daily.title: Facing a tough problem
daily.description: Talking to yourself over difficult homework.
daily.example: A problem this hard — how am I supposed to solve it?

daily.title: Complaining in a chat
daily.description: Talking with a friend about never-ending construction.
daily.example: Who knows when the construction in front of the station will ever end.

daily.title: Looking for something
daily.description: Mom mutters while hunting for her keys.
daily.example: Where did I put my keys? I can't remember at all.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character feels helpless about the situation.
daily.example: I can't even guess what will happen from here on.

work.title: Stalled project
work.description: Coworkers discuss a project's prospects.
work.example: Now the budget's been cut too — who knows what'll become of this project.

work.title: Reading an opinion piece
work.description: An article doubts a policy.
work.example: Whether this policy will actually work remains in doubt.

work.title: Grumbling with a coworker
work.description: Frustration with a boss who keeps changing plans. Only among close colleagues.
work.example: What does the manager even want? The policy changed again.

etymology: 「やら」 is a contraction of 「にやあらむ」 (“is it perhaps …?”), passing through 「やらん」 to 「やら」, and itself carries an uncertain, questioning tone. The 「の」, 「もの」 and 「こと」 before it are formal nouns.
formation: 「やら」 is generally thought to come from the old 「にやあらむ」 (“it is …, I suppose?”) and itself carries an uncertain, questioning tone. The preceding 「の」, 「もの」 or 「こと」 is a formal noun that packages the clause into “the fact that ….” Together it means “how is it, I wonder?” — a question is thrown out with no one to ask and no answer expected, so it becomes a self-addressed “I wonder …”; precisely because no answer can come, worry and resignation naturally colour the tone. The three forms differ by the formal noun: 「の」 is the most general; 「もの」 carries the sense of “what one should do” and mostly asks about method (どうしたものやら); 「こと」 refers to a state of affairs about to happen and mostly expresses worry about the future (どうなることやら).

similar.title: 〜のやら〜のやら
similar.explanation: Both come from 「やら」, which expresses uncertainty. 「AのやらBのやら」 lists two possibilities: “I don't know whether A or B”; this grammar point voices doubt about one matter only.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: 「のだろうか」 is a neutral question or self-question, and can also pose a question in writing; 「のやら」 carries stronger resignation, bewilderment and dissatisfaction, and is mostly a spoken mutter to oneself.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: 「かな」 is a light self-question, “I wonder …”, emotionally neutral, and can be said to others; 「のやら」 mostly carries complaint or resignation and is a mutter to oneself.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: They share 「やら」, but 「AやらBやら」 is a listing meaning “both … and …”, as in 「泣くやら笑うやら」, and does not express a question.

meaning: Lists two opposite or different possibilities: “whether … or …, who knows”. Shows confusion or annoyance.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form + のやら + plain form + のやら (na-adjective / noun: なのやら)

senses.label: Yes or no?
senses.meaning: Pairs the positive and negative of the same action: “can't tell whether they will or not”. Often shows annoyance at someone being vague. Often followed by 「わからない」 or 「はっきりしない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のやら + verb nai-form + のやら
examples: He won't say clearly whether he's coming or not.
I have no idea whether my son is studying or not.

senses.label: A or B?
senses.meaning: Lists two different states or possibilities that are hard to tell apart. Often used for someone who is hard to read.
senses.connection: Plain form A + のやら + plain form B + のやら
examples: I can't tell from her face whether she's happy or angry.
I never know if he's serious or joking.

notes: 「の」 is required. Without 「の」, 「AやらBやら」 is a listing meaning “both … and …”, as in 「泣くやら笑うやら」, which is a completely different meaning.
Na-adjectives and nouns need 「な」: ✕「本気のやら冗談のやら」→ ○「本気なのやら冗談なのやら」.
It carries dissatisfaction with someone's vague attitude. Saying 「やる気があるのやらないのやら」 to a superior or colleague is criticism and very rude.

daily.title: Waiting for a friend's reply
daily.description: A friend still hasn't said if they're coming to the party.
daily.example: That guy won't even reply — no idea if he's coming or not.

daily.title: A child's reaction
daily.description: Parents can't tell if their child likes the present.
daily.example: Hard to tell whether he likes the present or not — he barely reacted.

work.title: Vague client
work.description: Reporting a client's reaction to the boss.
work.example: It's unclear whether they intend to sign the contract or not.

work.title: Reading a news commentary
work.description: A commentator criticizes the government's vague stance.
work.example: The government is avoiding a clear answer on whether it will raise taxes or not.

etymology: The doubtful 「やら」 (from 「にやあらむ」) follows the nominalizer 「の」 to make 「のやら」. Placing two of them side by side shows being unable to decide between two possibilities.

similar.title: 〜のやら・〜ものやら・〜ことやら
similar.explanation: Both come from the same source. The single 「のやら」 voices doubt about one matter; 「AのやらBのやら」 lists two possibilities and means you cannot tell which.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「やら」 is shared, but 「AやらBやら」 has no 「の」 and is a listing meaning “both … and …”, as in 「泣くやら笑うやら」. This grammar point has 「の」 and means “I don't know whether A or B”.

similar.title: 〜かどうか
similar.explanation: 「かどうか」 is a neutral “whether or not”, often used in 「〜かどうかわからない」. 「のやら〜のやら」 means something similar but carries the speaker's bewilderment and dissatisfaction.

formation: 「のやら」 is made of 「やら」, which expresses “uncertainty” (generally thought to come from the old 「にやあらむ」), plus the formal noun 「の」, meaning “is it perhaps …?”. Placing two 「のやら」 side by side makes two self-questions: “is it A? or is it B?”. Neither question gets an answer; the speaker swings between the two possibilities, which gives the sense “which on earth it is, I can't tell”. The most typical case sets an affirmative against a negative (来るのやら来ないのやら), and pushing the wavering to the extreme brings out dissatisfaction with the other person's vague attitude.

meaning: Something important is coming up soon: “with … just ahead”. It can also mean physically having something close behind.
connection: Noun + を (time word + に) 控えて / 控えた + noun

senses.label: With … coming up
senses.meaning: An important event — an exam, a match, a wedding — is just around the corner. Often 「AをBに控えて」, where B is a time word like “tomorrow” or “next month”. The second part is usually preparation or current feelings.
senses.connection: Noun + を + time word + に控えて; noun + を控えた + noun
examples: With the entrance exam tomorrow, my son is nervous.
My sister, whose wedding is next month, seems busy every day.
With the final coming up, the players began their last preparations.

senses.label: Written: 〜を控え、
senses.meaning: News reports often use the continuative 「〜を控え、」. It describes what is happening on the eve of a major event.
senses.connection: Noun + を控え、+ clause
examples: With the general election approaching, the parties are becoming more active.
With the shareholders' meeting coming up, management is scrambling to prepare.

senses.label: Backed by, close to
senses.meaning: Something like a mountain or the sea is right behind or next to a place. Mostly in written descriptions of scenery.
senses.connection: (背後に) 山 / 海 + を控えた + noun
examples: It's a quiet hot-spring town with mountains at its back.

notes: 「控える」 also means “to refrain, to avoid”, and the preceding noun decides the meaning: 「試験を控えて」 is “with the exam coming up”, while 「お酒を控えて」 is “cutting down on alcohol”. Misreading it changes the meaning completely.
What precedes must be an important upcoming event with a clear date; do not use it for everyday trifles: ✕「昼ご飯を控えて準備する」 (this would be understood as “eat less lunch”).

The signs common in Japan, 「撮影はお控えください」 and 「通話はお控えください」, are polite prohibitions (“please refrain from …”). That is the “refrain” meaning, not this grammar point. Follow them, or you will be very rude.

daily.title: Nervous before an exam
daily.description: A student explains how they've been lately.
daily.example: With the entrance exam a week away, I can't even sleep at night.

daily.title: Family news
daily.description: Telling a relative that your sister is about to give birth.
daily.example: My sister is due soon, so she's come back to stay with our parents.

work.title: Reading the news
work.description: A report on the eve of a sports event.
work.example: With the opening just days away, preparations at the venue are moving at full speed.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Explaining to a client why the company is busy.
work.example: We are currently preparing for a new product launch, so our responses are delayed.

etymology: 「控える」 originally means “to wait nearby, to stand by”. From “something is waiting right beside you” came “something is about to happen” and, spatially, “close by”. Separately it developed the meaning “to hold back, to refrain”.

similar.title: 〜に先立って
similar.explanation: 「に先立って」 means “before …, (do something first)” and focuses on the action taken beforehand, as in 「開会に先立って挨拶する」; 「を控えて」 focuses on the state and feelings of an event being imminent.

similar.title: 〜に向けて
similar.explanation: 「に向けて」 means preparing with an upcoming event as the goal and focuses on the direction of effort; 「を控えて」 stresses that the event is right in front of you, with more time pressure.

similar.title: 〜矢先に
similar.explanation: 「矢先に」 means just as someone is about to do something, something unexpected happens, and what follows is usually surprising; 「を控えて」 only states that something is near, with no hint of surprise.

formation: 「控える」 originally means “to wait nearby, to stand by” (for example 「控え室」 is a waiting room). 「Aを控える」 is “having A stand by at one's side”: the event waits next to you like a performer in the wings, so it means “A is about to come”. In 「AをBに控えて」, 「に」 marks “until which day it stands by”, i.e., on day B it will come on stage. The same image of “standing guard at one's side”, applied to space, gives “with mountains behind, facing the sea”; applied to one's own conduct, it means “leaving the act aside and not doing it”, that is, “refrain, avoid”.

meaning: “Taking … as an opportunity”: something becomes the trigger to start a new action or make a change.
connection: Noun + を機に / を機として; verb ta-form + の + を機に

senses.label: Taking … as a chance
senses.meaning: A turning point in life or society becomes the chance to start something new or make a change. Usually a positive, deliberate decision. More formal than 「をきっかけに」.
senses.connection: Noun + を機に (結婚, 就職, 退職, 転勤, 入学); 〜たの + を機に
examples: When I got married, I quit my job and moved back to my hometown.
Getting sick was my chance to quit smoking.
When I joined the company, I started living on my own.

senses.label: Taking this opportunity
senses.meaning: 「これを機に」 is a common set phrase. Used in speeches and letters: “taking this opportunity, (from now on) …”.
senses.connection: これ + を機に + 今後とも / ぜひ etc.
examples: Taking this opportunity, we look forward to working with you in the future.
Why not take this opportunity to rethink your health?

notes: What follows is a change or decision you actively make using the occasion. For naturally occurring changes (especially bad ones), use 「を境に」: ✕「事故を機に体調が悪くなった」→ ○「事故を境に体調が悪くなった」.
A verb clause must be nominalized first: ✕「結婚したを機に」→ ○「結婚したのを機に」.
「機」 is read 「き」, not 「はた」. 「これを機に」 is a proper phrase for speeches and business emails, as in 「これを機に、今後ともよろしくお願いいたします」.

daily.title: Explaining a move
daily.description: Telling a friend why you moved.
daily.example: When our kid started elementary school, we moved to the suburbs.

daily.title: New Year's resolution
daily.description: Chatting with family about your plans for the year.
daily.example: With the new year, I've decided to go jogging every morning.

work.title: Farewell speech
work.description: A speech at a farewell party for a transfer.
work.example: With this transfer, I want to take on new fields as well.

work.title: Business email
work.description: A greeting after a first collaboration.
work.example: Taking this opportunity, we sincerely hope for a long relationship.

etymology: 「機」 means “opportunity, the right moment”, as in 「機会」 and 「契機」. 「を機に」 is literally “taking … as the moment”.

similar.title: 〜をきっかけに
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning. 「きっかけ」 is more colloquial, can be used for small chance events, and what follows may be a change you did not initiate; 「を機に」 is more formal and mostly a decision actively made at a turning point in life.

similar.title: 〜を契機に
similar.explanation: 「契機」 and 「機」 share a source, both meaning “opportunity”. 「を契機に」 is the most written and mostly used for big changes in society or history; 「を機に」 is often used for personal decisions and in business.

similar.title: 〜を境に
similar.explanation: 「を境に」 stresses a sharp change before and after a point, and the change is mostly natural; 「を機に」 stresses using the occasion to start a new action on purpose.

formation: 「機」 means “timing, opportunity” (as in 「機会」「好機」「契機」). In 「Aを機に」, 「を」 picks out the object, and 「に」 can be seen as a shortened form of the 「として」 in 「を機として」, literally “taking A as the opportunity”. An “opportunity” implies “seizing it to do something”, so what follows is naturally a new action or decision the speaker takes actively. This differs from 「を境に」, which stresses a dividing line: 「境」 is just a line and changes can occur naturally, whereas 「機」 is a chance that someone must seize.

meaning: “With … as the dividing line”: things change clearly before and after a point. It can also mark a physical boundary.
connection: Noun + を境に(して) / を境として

senses.label: Turning point
senses.meaning: Before and after a certain time or event, things are completely different. The second part is usually “changed completely” or “started to …”. The change often just happens, not necessarily by choice.
senses.connection: Time / event noun + を境に(して) (あの日, 事故, その日, 震災)
examples: Ever since that accident, he became a completely different person.
Once I turned 40, my stamina suddenly dropped.
From that day on, the two stopped speaking to each other.

senses.label: Boundary line
senses.meaning: A river, mountain range or road serves as a physical boundary. The second part is usually “is divided into …” or “is different”.
senses.connection: Place noun + を境に (川, 山, 県境, 道路)
examples: With this river as the border, the east is Osaka and the west is Hyogo.
The weather is completely different on either side of the mountains.

notes: What follows must be a clear contrast or difference between before and after; a single action will not do: ✕「卒業を境に旅行した」→ ○「卒業を機に旅行した」／「卒業を境に生活が一変した」.
「境」 is read 「さかい」 here, not 「きょう」 (that reading is used in 「国境」 and 「境界」).
For a decision you make deliberately, 「を機に」 is more natural; what follows 「を境に」 is mostly a change that happens naturally and is out of your control.

daily.title: Looking back
daily.description: Telling a friend how you changed.
daily.example: Studying abroad really changed the way I think.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Small talk with a neighbor as the seasons change.

etymology: 「境」 means “border, boundary”, as in 「国境」 and 「県境」. 「を境に」 is literally “taking … as the border”, extended from physical boundaries to points in time.

similar.title: 〜を機に
similar.explanation: 「を機に」 mostly means using the occasion to start a new action; 「を境に」 stresses that the state before and after the point is completely different, and the change is mostly natural.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: 「てからというもの」 follows the te-form of a verb and stresses “ever since …, always …”, with a continuing state afterward; 「を境に」 follows a noun and stresses the contrast before and after the dividing point.

similar.title: 〜を皮切りに
similar.explanation: 「を皮切りに」 means starting with this, similar things happen one after another, as in tours and store openings; 「を境に」 means that things change before and after this point.

similar.title: 〜を限りに
similar.explanation: 「を限りに」 means a certain point in time is the last, and things do not continue afterward, as in 「今日を限りに引退する」; 「を境に」 only says before and after are different and does not mean “this is the end”.

formation: 「境」 means “boundary, border” (as in 「県境」「境目」). 「Aを境に」 literally means “taking A as the boundary line”, with 「に」 marking it as the reference. The main job of a boundary line is to separate the two sides, so this expression focuses on the contrast between “this side of the line” and “that side”: in space, the two sides belong to different areas; in time, the states before and after an event are sharply different. Because the “line” itself does nothing, the change often occurs naturally, unlike 「を機に」, where someone must act on purpose.

meaning: Means “on the premise of ~” and builds the following action or judgment on it; it can also modify a noun (〜を前提とした) or say “~ is a prerequisite” (〜が前提だ).
connection: Noun + を前提として／を前提に; noun + を前提とした／を前提とする + noun; plain form + こと + を前提に; noun + が前提だ／が前提となる
etymology: 「前提」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “prerequisite”, originally a logic term (the starting point of an argument). 「〜を前提とする」 means “to take … as the premise”; 「として」 is the te-form of 「とする」.
formation: It is made of 「を」 + the Sino-Japanese noun 「前提」 + 「に（して）／として」, an application of the 「AをBにする／AをBとする」 pattern (to treat A as B). 「前提」 is originally a term from logic, meaning a condition set in advance for reasoning. 「Aを前提に」 means “putting A in the position of premise”, and the actions and judgments that follow rest on A holding true. Before a noun it becomes 「を前提とした／にした + noun」; conversely, when A is the subject, you say 「Aが前提だ／Aが前提となる」.

senses.label: On the premise of
senses.meaning: Doing something, dating someone, or making a plan with a certain condition as the basis. Formal and written. 「を前提に」 is also common.
senses.connection: Noun + を前提として / を前提に + verb
examples: Please go out with me with marriage in mind.
This system operates on the condition that the person consents.

senses.label: … premised on …
senses.meaning: 「〜を前提とした + noun」 and 「〜を前提とする + noun」 modify a noun: “… based on the premise of …”.
senses.connection: Noun + を前提とした / を前提とする + noun
examples: This curriculum is designed for students planning to study abroad.
This training assumes you will be hired as a full-time employee.

senses.label: Assuming that …
senses.meaning: With 「〜ことを前提に」, you first assume a situation is true and then plan or judge. Common in business and academic settings.
senses.connection: Plain form + こと + を前提として / を前提に
examples: We made the plan assuming everyone would take part.
We need to draw up the budget on the assumption that prices will rise.

senses.label: Is a prerequisite
senses.meaning: 「〜が前提だ」 and 「〜が前提となる」 mean something is a necessary condition. Without it, things can't go ahead.
senses.connection: Noun + が前提だ／が前提となる
examples: Advance registration is required to participate.
This system requires the person's own consent.

notes: 「結婚を前提にお付き合いしてください」 is a very serious request to start dating, meaning you are earnestly considering marriage. Saying it casually puts great pressure on the other person and sounds careless.
A verb clause must be nominalized with 「こと」: ✕「全員が参加するを前提に」→ ○「全員が参加することを前提に」or「全員が参加するという前提で」.
Particles are easy to get wrong: ✕「を前提で」→ ○「を前提に」「という前提で」.
When 「前提」 is the predicate, the particle is 「が」: ✕ 「本人の同意を前提だ」 → ○ 「本人の同意が前提だ」／「本人の同意を前提とする」.
「前提」 mostly refers to a condition or assumption set in advance. To act on facts or results already obtained, 「を踏まえて」 is usually used, as in 「調査結果を踏まえて改善案を作った」.

similar.title: 〜を踏まえて
similar.explanation: 「を踏まえて」 means acting on existing facts, results or opinions; 「を前提として」 is mostly based on conditions set in advance or assumptions not yet confirmed.

similar.title: 〜をもとに(して)
similar.explanation: 「をもとに」 means making something using something as material or basis, as in 「実話をもとにした映画」; 「を前提として」 means acting with some condition as a prerequisite, not using it as material.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: 「〜に基づいて」 means acting on the basis of rules, data, and so on. 「〜を前提に」 stresses setting a condition first and making every arrangement on the premise that it holds.
